analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the Affordable Care Act's annual fee on health insurance companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with support from two Republicans and a Democrat, never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Care Act charges health insurance companies an annual fee on the premiums they collect. This bill would erase that fee permanently. Insurance companies say the fee is built into the premiums customers pay, so sponsors framed the repeal as protection for patients. But because the fee also brings money into the federal Treasury — money used in part to help pay for the very premium subsidies that keep coverage affordable — eliminating it means insurers keep more while the government takes in less.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurance companies gain the most: the annual fee they pay under the Affordable Care Act (which was suspended for 2019 and set to return in 2020) would disappear permanently, directly increasing their after-tax income. Some people who buy insurance on their own without a government subsidy could see modestly lower premiums to the extent insurers pass the savings through rather than keeping it. People whose premiums are paid in part by federal tax credits would see no benefit, since their subsidy is tied to the price of coverage — any savings would flow back to insurers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 9010 of the Affordable Care Act, the annual fee imposed on health insurance providers, removing the charge entirely.
Sponsors titled the relevant section 'Protecting Patients from Higher Premiums,' reflecting their argument that insurers build the fee into what customers pay, so repeal would ease premiums.
Because the fee was already suspended for 2019 under existing law and scheduled to be reimposed in 2020, the bill's practical effect was to make the industry's one-year break permanent.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays, giving up the revenue the fee raises every year — revenue that helps finance premium tax credits for people buying coverage on their own. Customers who buy insurance with federal subsidies pay too, in the form of savings that go to insurers rather than to them. If insurers pass little of the repealed fee through to lower premiums, unsubsidized customers also gain little while the industry keeps the windfall.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and subsidized customers

drawbacks.text: The fee raises federal revenue; repealing it removes that money from the Treasury, which under current law uses revenue including the fee to help fund premium tax credits that keep coverage affordable for ordinary buyers.

People whose premiums are subsidized through the Affordable Care Act would not benefit from repeal: their subsidies are pegged to premium prices, so if insurers lower premiums, the federal government saves rather than the customer — meaning the industry captures the money.
The bill leaves repeal of the fee entirely to insurers, with no requirement that the savings reach customers through lower premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main, guaranteed beneficiary of repeal is the insurance industry, which gets a permanent multi-billion-dollar annual fee removed; the stated benefit for patients depends entirely on insurers voluntarily passing the savings into premiums, with no mechanism in the bill to require it. For subsidized customers — a large share of the individual market — the arithmetic runs the other way: their premiums are already mostly paid by tax credits, so lower premiums save the government money, not the household. The bill is best understood as a tax cut for a specific industry wrapped in patient-protection language, and it never included a way to pay for the lost revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died without a vote when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 10, 2019 by Senator Barrasso, joined in the introduction by Senator Gardner (R) and Senator Sinema (D).
On the day of introduction it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote appear in the bill's action history for the remainder of the Congress.
The fee it sought to repeal was suspended for 2019 under existing law and scheduled to return in 2020, so the bill's failure meant the fee stayed on the books.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the annual fee remained in the tax code and the revenue it raises stayed available to the Treasury. Health insurers had already received a one-year holiday in 2019 under separately enacted law, and they would have made that break permanent had this bill passed — instead, the status quo held. The outcome is best described as a rare case where a bill favoring a concentrated interest simply expired quietly, though the fee's return in 2020 meant the cost continued to be embedded in premiums and federal subsidy spending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal Treasury, which kept the fee revenue

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in two years, despite its bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan at introduction — two Republicans and a Democrat sponsored it, and the six cosponsors split 5 Republicans and 1 Democrat — but the bill also drew no recorded opposition, and no chamber ever voted on it.

industries.note: Repeal would have permanently removed the annual fee insurers owe under the Affordable Care Act, adding billions of dollars a year to their after-tax income. Insurers argue the fee is passed through to premiums, so repeal could lower prices for unsubsidized customers — but the bill imposed no requirement that savings reach customers, and customers whose premiums are paid by federal tax credits would capture none of it, since any premium reduction would lower the subsidy the government pays rather than the bill the household owes.

Repeal would have eliminated the fee's revenue with no offset, increasing the deficit. Because much of the fee's incidence is built into premiums that federal tax credits help pay, repeal would shift money from the Treasury to insurers on policies the government subsidizes.
